steps.action: Set out the published rival positions on Red River fault hazard: the fault is inactive with no large-earthquake risk, or it is locked and in a seismogenic stage.
steps.quote: some researchers believe that the role of the Red River fault as the west boundary of the Sichuan-Yunnan block has weakened

steps.action: Posed the question of which faults in the middle-northern Red River fault region carry large stress accumulations and what deformation mechanism they reflect.
steps.quote: It is still unknown which faults have developed large stress accumulations in the majority of the area

steps.action: Designed a zoned analysis by dividing the study area into three tectonic units (north extensional, middle strike-slip, west complex rupture) based on fault activity and focal mechanism types.
steps.quote: we divided the target area into three structural units

steps.action: Collected focal mechanism solutions of M > 5.0 earthquakes from 1976 to 2000 from the China Earthquake Data Center catalog.
steps.quote: were collected from the China Earthquake Data Center

steps.action: Inverted focal mechanisms of 2000-2019 moderate earthquakes with the CAP method (F-K Green's functions, Pnl and surface-wave windows, Butterworth filtering), grid-searching strike, dip, rake and centroid depth.
steps.quote: the optimal dual force couple solution of fault strike, slip angle, and dip angle is searched at different depths

steps.action: Mapped the faulting-type distribution: normal faulting in the north extensional area, strike-slip in the middle area, and mixed strike-slip and thrust in the Baoshan-Tengchong block.
steps.quote: normal fault-type earthquakes were primarily concentrated in the north extensional area, with tensile characteristics

steps.action: Projected P and T axes horizontally to estimate principal compressive stress directions in each unit (NW-NNW deflecting to NNW southward; NE-SW and NNW in the west).
steps.quote: the direction of the principal compressive stress was deflected to the NNW along the fault from north to south

steps.action: Compared the stress directions with earlier regional stress-field studies and reported agreement.
steps.quote: This result is consistent with previous research findings

steps.action: Corrected SH spectra of 5221 ML 1.5-5.5 events (2009-2020) for path, site and instrument effects, applied station, SNR and fit-error criteria, fitted an omega-square spectrum, and computed Brune stress drops per inversion area.
steps.quote: the Brune model was used to calculate the focal stress drop from a small-moderate earthquake

steps.action: Checked the stress-drop estimates against the known regularity that mean stress drop increases with magnitude (Table 1), and used it to set the comparison principle.
steps.quote: mean stress drop increases with increasing earthquake size

steps.action: Binned stress drops at 4 MPa intervals and mapped them. High-stress-drop events concentrate in the Lijiang-Jianchuan to Weixi-Qiaohou transition, Lanping-Yunlong, Chuxiong to Qujiang, and Changning-Baoshan-Yongping. Low drops appear in the Lijiang focal area. The authors read high drops as accumulated stress.
steps.quote: High-stress-drop earthquakes extended from the Chuxiong fault (F10) to the Qujiang fault (F11)

steps.action: Listed five published rival kinematic models for the dynamic mechanism of northwestern Yunnan.
steps.quote: There were many opposing viewpoints on the dynamic stress mechanism in northwestern Yunnan

steps.action: Judged the focal-mechanism and stress-drop findings consistent with model 5 (clockwise subblock rotation and EW extension, Wu et al. 2008).
steps.quote: This study’s findings are consistent with the kinematic model of view

steps.action: Revised model 5 by grouping the Deqin-Zhongdian-Daju fault with the NW dextral strike-slip faults rather than the sinistral NE faults (Fig. 7b).
steps.quote: the authors preferred to associate the Deqin-Zhongdian-Daju fault with the Weixi-Qiaohou fault (F3)

steps.action: Compared P axes with the published GPS strain field, and NW- and SN-trending faults with velocity-structure low-speed anomalies, reporting correspondence.
steps.quote: which agrees with the GPS strain field (Chen et al., 2012)

steps.action: Kept a unit-by-unit kinematic model: NW dextral faults accommodate the SE-SSE block motion in the north, SN sinistral faults do so in the middle, and rotation with NE sinistral faults does so in the west.
steps.quote: also accommodated the SE-SSE movement of the Sichuan-Yunnan block by the dextral strike-slip movement of the NW fault

steps.action: Combined cited GPS rates (middle area faster than north), stress drops of 20 MPa or more in low-velocity zones, cited locking depths, b-values and paleoseismic evidence to argue that the middle section drives passive deformation in the north and across the fault.
steps.quote: the motion rate of movement for the middle strike-slip movement area was greater than that of the north extensional area

steps.action: Concluded that middle-section slip and rotation may drive passive deformation of the north section, and that large-earthquake risk in the middle-northern Red River fault should be monitored.
steps.quote: the potential risk of a large earthquake in the middle-northern section of the Red River fault should be monitored

end.claim: High stress drops mark local stress accumulation, and strike slip and rotation of the Red River fault's middle section may drive passive deformation of the north section, so the middle-northern fault carries large-earthquake risk that should be monitored.

decisive_move.sentence: Without the Brune stress-drop inversion of 5221 small and moderate earthquakes there would be no map of high-stress-drop zones on which the accumulation and passive-deformation claims rest.

gates.evidence: The data are routine network waveforms and catalog solutions, not acquired under a stated hypothesis (p. 73). The kinematic model is judged only 'consistent' with the data, without predictions derived for rival models (p. 75). The 4 MPa bins and selection thresholds are not stated as fixed before the analysis (p. 73).

limits: The supplied XML contains only the abstract and captions, so body text is cited by printed pages. No uncertainties are given for stress drops, corner frequencies or stress-axis directions. No sensitivity tests are reported for shear velocity, the Brune constant k, filter bands, the SNR or fit-error thresholds, or the 4 MPa binning. The velocity-structure inversion, and the 'seismic relocation' cited for Fig. 5, are never described; inference: they come from other or unreported work. The five rival kinematic models are not given distinct predictions, so the choice of model 5 is an assertion of consistency, not a test. Agreement with prior stress-field, GPS and velocity studies is stated qualitatively, and the comparison was not re-performed with those data here. These checks are coded as replication with performed_here false; a reader could argue they are comparisons performed here. Reading stress drop as a stress-accumulation proxy is a premise taken from cited work. Sub-claims and their statuses: stress-axis directions per unit, estimate without stated resolution (weaker than estimate_with_resolution); location of high-stress-drop zones, the same; passive deformation crossing the fault and risk in the middle-north section, best_explanation and speculative ('may', 'could indicate'). Composition trace_series fits only loosely: there are no varied auxiliaries, and the rivals are cited, not tested. No review file was supplied, so no review sequence is coded and tree question 9 is not answered.

disagreements.quote: This does not imply that the strong earthquake risk in the Red River fault’s middle and north sections will be reduced in the future.
